title: Copied in on everything
text: {~Your manager|The person you report to} has started {~asking for a status update before lunch|copying themselves into every email|standing behind your desk}. {~Your work hasn't changed. Their anxiety has.|You are starting to dread the sound of their shoes.}

outcomes.text: I sent a summary every morning. After a month they stopped checking, and I kept sending them out of habit.
It fed the beast. They wanted more, and I became the person who always answered within a minute.
They were embarrassed and then grateful. Things eased. I think they'd never been asked.
They said they'd 'reflect', then did the same thing more quietly.
It went around the office by lunchtime. My name was used in a sentence beginning 'Apparently'.
I updated my CV at the kitchen table, and the act of it felt like opening a window.
A recruiter called before I'd finished the first draft. The timing felt like a sign.

title: The boss who is better than you
text: {~Your manager|The head of your team} {~rewrote your report in the margin, and they were right|handled a client call in a way you'll be analysing for weeks|says your ideas are 'fine'}. You've never felt so sharpened and so stupid.

outcomes.text: I spent a year a pace behind, and learned more than in any course.
They let me sit in on two meetings and then forgot. I made the most of the two.
They thought for a moment and said 'you may be right'. I'll be living off that for years.
I was wrong, and it was public, and educational.
Safe and dull. I learned the minimum and felt the lack.
Quietly, I got better just by watching. It took two years and nobody noticed.

title: A rival in the next desk
text: {~A colleague|Someone two desks along} has started {~getting invited to meetings you're not|saying 'we' when they mean themselves|competing with you on everything, including who arrives first}.

outcomes.text: I won the quarter and lost a weekend. They sent me a small, sincere message of congratulation.
I wore myself out and they got the client anyway. I deserved better, which is not how it works.
We had a coffee. It turned out they were as scared as I was. We became the closest pair on the floor.
They took the coffee and used the conversation in the next meeting against me.
The director listened, nodded, and did nothing visible. A month later my rival's budget shrank.
It got back to them before it got to anyone else. The atmosphere on the floor changed.

title: You have been told something
text: {~A colleague|The office gossip} lowers their voice and tells you {~who is being let go|who earns what|that two senior people are in a relationship|what the director really said}.

outcomes.text: It was heavy to carry, but by spring nobody remembered who knew it first.
I accidentally let it slip in a meeting. Someone looked at me very carefully.
I got a moment of popularity and then a long hangover of regret.
It went round the floor like a virus. I was found out within a week.

choices.label: Tell them you'd rather not know

outcomes.text: They looked hurt, then relieved. We've never discussed it again.
They told me anyway, in a corridor, in four words.

title: Someone is paying attention
text: {~A senior colleague|A manager from another team} has been {~quietly sending you useful articles|stopping by your desk to ask how it's going|putting your name forward for things}.

choices.label: Ask them to mentor you properly

outcomes.text: We met monthly for two years. It was the best professional decision I ever made.
They said yes, and their calendar said no. We managed four meetings.
I took the tips and never said thank you. I regret that.
I sent a card at Christmas. They kept it on their desk for years.
I wanted to do it my own way. It was slower.
They respected it, and left the door open.

title: A vote on industrial action
text: {~The union has called a ballot|Your colleagues are talking about a walk-out|A notice on the board proposes a strike}, over {~pay|staffing|a change to the pension|a rota nobody agreed to}.

outcomes.text: The picket line was cold and oddly joyful. We won most of what we asked for.
The strike went on for weeks. The company held out. We went back with less than we'd hoped.
I crossed the line and was spat at in a car park. The company thanked me in an email.
The vote failed without me. I kept working and felt the looks for a year.
I stayed out of it. The outcome was a compromise that pleased nobody, which is usually how you can tell it's fair.
Nobody asked me why, which is how I found out I wasn't as central as I'd thought.

title: The all-hands meeting
text: A meeting is called at short notice. {~The director's smile is a little too steady.|There are pastries, which is always a bad sign.|Everyone has brought a notebook and nobody is writing.}

outcomes.text: The package was better than I'd feared. I left with a cheque and a card and a clean feeling.
I took it, and three months later the same company was hiring for my old role at less.
By the time the letters went round, I already had two interviews. I kept my head up.
I found nothing and felt the clock in my chest.
I picked up the work of two people who'd left. They noticed, eventually.
I worked twice as hard and was let go anyway in the next round.
The wave passed over me. I've felt vaguely guilty about my luck ever since.

title: A seat at the right table
text: {~A senior person|The director} has noticed you, and {~wants you in the room for the big presentation|suggested you lead the new project|put your name on a list}. {~It might be a break. It might be a trap.|Everybody is watching to see what you do with it.}

outcomes.text: I rehearsed for a week. It went better than I dared hope, and I was promoted by summer.
It went wrong in a small, instructive way. They forgave me because they'd forgiven themselves worse.
My team loved me for it, and the director noted the gesture. Modesty, it turns out, is a tactic.
The director liked the confidence of a solo act more. I was quietly passed over.
I sent someone deserving. They never forgot it, and later returned the favour.
They thanked me and did not offer again.

title: An invoice that never gets paid
text: A client is {~sixty days|ninety days|four months} late paying a {~large|rather important|frankly life-sustaining} invoice, and every email you send gets a cheerful auto-reply.

outcomes.text: On the fifth email they paid, with an apology so warm I almost felt I'd been rude.
They paid a third of it and promised the rest. The rest is, as I write, still promised.
I told myself I was buying a lesson. It was an expensive one.
I wrote it off and spent a month telling myself it was fine. It wasn't, but it was over.
A letter from a solicitor worked in a day. I got paid, and lost the client. I'd have made the same call again.
The company had gone into administration. The demand reached no one.

title: The big client
text: {~A larger company|A client with a recognisable name} wants to {~retain you for six months|give you a proper, long-term contract}. The rate is {~half again your usual|more money than you've asked for in one go}.

outcomes.text: Six months of steady work, and steady pay. I also stopped looking for other clients, which bit me at the end.
The contract was renewed, then cancelled with a week's notice. I had no pipeline.

choices.label: Take it, but keep other clients

outcomes.text: I ran myself ragged and ended up earning more than I ever had. I slept like the dead.
Something slipped, and a small client left in a huff. A price worth paying, I think.
They came up again, and I learned how much I'd been under-charging for years.
They said no and went elsewhere. I've thought about the extra 10% every day since.

title: Is this it?
text: You're {~in a meeting|on the train home|in the kitchen at 6 a.m.} and the thought arrives, fully formed: {~'I could do something else.'|'I've been doing this for fifteen years.'|'What if I'd been wrong about what I wanted?'}

outcomes.text: Two years of night classes. It nearly broke my marriage, and then it rebuilt it.
I quit after six months. The notes are still in a drawer, and sometimes I open it.
I resigned on a Friday and felt my shoulders drop an inch. I've never looked back.
I quit, and the first six months were a disaster. The next three years were wonderful.

choices.label: Stay, and change what you can

outcomes.text: I asked for a transfer. Three weeks later I was in a different team and a slightly different life.
Nothing changed, except that I now knew what I was putting up with.

title: A call from a recruiter
text: A recruiter has {~your number and a pitch|found you online|heard good things about you from someone you don't know}. The job is {~more money, less interesting|the same work at a better company|something you've never done and a bit terrifying}.

outcomes.text: I got the offer. I used it to ask for a raise at my current job, which I got.
The interview went better than expected and the job turned out to be a different one from the brief.
They checked back in a year. By then I was ready.
I never heard from them again, and sometimes I wonder about the other path.

choices.label: Let it slip to your boss

outcomes.text: It worked. I got a raise and a slightly uncomfortable hug.
It did not work. My boss said 'Good luck', and meant it.

title: Another month of searching
text: {~The emails have stopped|The auto-replies are all the same|The CV feels like a work of fiction} and the gap on it is getting harder to explain.

choices.label: Ask a friend for a referral

outcomes.text: A friend pushed my CV to the top of a pile. I got an interview because of a name, not a line.
The friend's company wasn't hiring. They felt awful, and so did I.
A stopgap job turned out to be fine. It also made the next application easier.
A stopgap job felt like a defeat. I worked it through gritted teeth.
Volunteering gave me a story to tell, and a reference.
It felt good, and did nothing to the CV, and I did it anyway.

title: 'Probably nothing'
text: The GP listened for two minutes, checked a screen and said it was {~probably stress|probably nothing|probably a virus}. You don't think it's {~stress|nothing|a virus}.

outcomes.text: They sighed and wrote the letter. It took a minute. I'd been dreading that minute for a week.
They referred me, reluctantly. The waiting list was long, but I was on it.
A different GP took it seriously the second time. The first was overstretched, not wrong.
The symptoms eased, and I felt both foolish and relieved.
A private clinic found it in an hour. The bill was not small.
They found nothing, and charged me for the privilege. At least I know now.

title: The letter that hasn't come
text: You're {~still waiting|keeping the hall table clear|checking the post} for the specialist's appointment. Every brown envelope makes your stomach drop.

outcomes.text: A receptionist found my name on a list I'd never have believed existed. A date was given, and it helped.
I was on hold for an hour and then told to 'wait for the letter'.
The consultant saw me within the week. The bill sat in my chest for a month.
Private was faster and no more certain. I'm not sure what I bought.

choices.label: Try not to think about it

outcomes.text: I threw myself into work, and was more productive than I'd been in years.
I couldn't stop thinking about it and lost a month to 3 a.m. searching.

title: Tired of taking them
text: It's the third year of the tablets. You {~feel fine|feel better than you did|can't remember the last flare} and the little box on the shelf is starting to feel like a verdict.

outcomes.text: For six months I felt great. Then the flare came back harder than before.
I got away with it for a year, but every twinge made me uneasy.
Boring, reliable, and exactly why I'm still well.
The side effects were real but manageable. I kept taking them, and resented them a little less each year.

choices.label: Talk it through with the doctor

outcomes.text: We lowered the dose. I felt no different and was told I was a model patient.
The doctor said a polite 'no', and was right, and I didn't enjoy it.

title: Holding the menu at arm's length
text: You find yourself {~holding the menu at arm's length|squinting at a screen|asking someone to read the small print}. {~They notice.|You're pretending it isn't happening.}

outcomes.text: The optician said 'quite common'. I felt like I was being admitted to a club.
The optician said 'you should have come two years ago'.

choices.label: Buy reading glasses at the chemist

outcomes.text: Three pairs, in different rooms, all of them lost by Friday.
They work. I look like my father. I'm at peace with it.
I gave myself a headache that lasted a week. A colleague laughed at me, kindly.
I missed a street sign and took a twenty-minute detour.

title: Three a.m., and a tooth
text: A tooth wakes you at {~three|half past two|four} in the morning and will not be reasoned with. {~You haven't seen a dentist in years.|It has been coming for months.}

outcomes.text: The dentist was kind and the bill was not. The relief was biblical.
They saw me within the hour and saved the tooth. I became a person who flosses.
Two days of painkillers and a swollen jaw. The tooth is lost now.
It eased off and I forgot about it, until the next time, which came worse.
An hour in the chair, a bill, a plan. I left feeling stupidly proud.
The dentist tutted at six separate things. I'm paying them off in instalments.

title: 'Turn it up'
text: Your {~family|partner|friends} keep asking you {~to repeat yourself|if you're all right|whether you've had your ears checked}. The television is now louder than is polite.

outcomes.text: The test said what I already knew. The audiologist was gentle about it.
They said it was age, and told me the options. I chose to think about it.
It didn't work, but it made for some good family arguments.
My daughter filmed me and played it back. It was funnier than it should have been.
A small beige object changed Sundays. I'd forgotten the sound of the kettle.
It took weeks to get used to. Then I heard my grandchild whisper my name.

title: The stairs are a negotiation
text: You {~climb a flight of stairs|run for the bus|play with the kids} and realise you {~have to stop halfway|are out of breath|can feel it in your knees}. {~That was not always true.|The stairs used to be nothing.}

outcomes.text: The first run was a disaster. The third was a good one. By spring I could do a parkrun without stopping.
I got shin splints in week three and stopped. I kept the trainers by the door as a reproach.

choices.label: Join a gym with a friend

outcomes.text: We went every Tuesday. We talked more than we lifted, and it was the best part of the week.
The friend dropped out after two weeks. I kept paying for three months.

choices.label: Tell yourself you'll start in January

outcomes.text: January came. I started in February.
I did start, eventually, and two years later I was glad I'd waited for nobody.

title: You can't remember the last good night
text: You're {~awake at 3 a.m. again|running on coffee|forgetting words mid-sentence}. The kind of tired that makes everything a little less bearable.

outcomes.text: No screens after ten, a book, a proper lamp. In three weeks I was sleeping like a teenager.
I lasted nine days. The habit is easy, and the discipline isn't.
The doctor asked five questions and put the answer on a leaflet. It was right.
They suggested therapy for the things keeping me awake. I went. It was a good idea.
A month later I snapped at someone who didn't deserve it. I'm apologising still.
I got through on caffeine and will. I am not proud of the price.

title: Forty
text: {~Forty|The fortieth birthday} arrives, {~and with it a specific pain in the lower back|with a card about being over the hill|and somebody kindly offers you a seat on the train}.

choices.label: Make a list of what you still want

outcomes.text: The list had eleven things on it. I crossed one off within the month.
The list was depressing. I burned it, then wrote a better one.
Everyone I love was in one room, which is rare. It was the best night of the decade.
Nobody came who I hoped would. The ones who did were brilliant.
It was a Tuesday. I went to work.
I got through the day. The next morning my back told me I hadn't got away with it.

title: Sixty
text: You are {~sixty|sixty today}, {~and it doesn't feel like what sixty was supposed to feel like|and still in possession of most of your marbles and a good number of your knees}.

outcomes.text: I sat with a notebook and a glass of wine. The decade started to look like a place you could go.
The plan fell apart on contact with reality, as plans do, but I'd had the thinking time.

choices.label: Travel somewhere you've always meant to

outcomes.text: I went to a place in a photograph on a wall I'd had since I was twenty. It was smaller and better.
The trip was harder than I'd planned for. My body reminded me of its terms. It was still worth it.
I walked to the park and sat on a bench and was perfectly content.
A quiet day, and a long phone call with someone I love.

title: Eighty
text: {~Eighty|Your eightieth year} and the {~stairs|garden|walk to the shops} are all a matter of {~planning|pace|negotiation}. {~The grandchildren are taller than you.|Somebody has said 'you don't look it' and they lied.}

outcomes.text: Four generations in one room. Nobody argued, which was a miracle.
They all came, stayed too long, left a mess. I'd have had it no other way.

choices.label: Write the letters you've meant to write

outcomes.text: It took a month. I left them with the solicitor. I slept better afterwards.
Halfway through, I found a letter I'd never sent in 1974. I sent it.
Normal is not a small thing at eighty. It's a gift.
I pretended it was just another day. A neighbour brought a cake, and I let them.

title: After the fall
text: It has been {~a few months|a long winter} since you fell, and {~you've stopped going down the stairs without the rail|the flat feels bigger and less safe|everyone has become very careful around you}.

outcomes.text: Rails, a stair lift and a walk-in shower. I felt old for a week and independent for years.
The installation took a month and was a nuisance, but the confidence was worth it.
I moved in two streets from my daughter. She pretended not to be thrilled, and I pretended not to be glad.
It was the right thing and I spent a year missing my old house.
I was fine for another year, and then I wasn't.
Stubbornness, I've found, is sometimes the very thing that keeps you going.

title: 'You look well'
text: {~A friend|Someone you haven't seen in years} tells you {~you look well|you don't look your age|they'd have thought you were ten years younger}. {~You try not to smile.|You realise it's true.}

outcomes.text: I listed them: walking, sleep, real food, not too much of the rest. They wrote them down.
I said 'it's just luck', and they said 'no it isn't'. They were right.
Compliments are a tax I'd pay every day if I could.
They said it again a year later. I finally believed it.

choices.label: Ask them to come with you next time

outcomes.text: They came for a walk and a coffee. It became a fortnightly thing.
They said yes, once, and never again. I understood.
